summary: Describes small but non-interoperable changes to DNS request and transaction signature records, SIG(0), which experience showed were necessary. It lets requests and responses be signed with a public key.

plainLanguage.summary: The older way of securing DNS protects the records a zone publishes, but says nothing about the request a client sent or the reply it got back. This RFC defines a signature that covers a whole exchange, so a client can be sure the answer really came from the server it asked and was not altered on the way.

questions: how long is a sig(0) valid
subtitle: How a DNS message can carry a public-key signature that proves who sent a request or answered it.

tldr.problem: Secure DNS in RFC 2535 protects data records but not requests, message headers or the overall integrity of a response. Implementation experience showed that the original SIG(0) rules needed fixing.
tldr.mechanism: A SIG(0) is a SIG record with a type covered field of zero, placed at the end of the additional information section. It signs the message, and for a response also the query that produced it, using a public key.
tldr.outcome: The changes are minor but not interoperable with RFC 2535. This document replaces the SIG(0) parts of RFC 2535, and its signature now also covers the inception and expiration times to resist replay.

facts.label: Time bracket
facts.value: Not more than 5 minutes past or future

facts.label: Signing key
facts.value: The host key, not the zone key

today: RFC 2931 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000. It updates RFC 2535, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its SIG(0) rules replace the corresponding parts of RFC 2535.

sections.title: What RFC 2931 Changes
sections.content:
This document makes minor but non-interoperable changes to part of RFC 2535, with which familiarity is assumed, and adds explanatory text. The changes concern the SIG resource records used to sign DNS requests and transactions, that is, request and response exchanges. Such a record is often called a SIG(0), because its type covered field is zero. The changes come from implementation and attempted implementation experience with TSIG in RFC 2845 and with the SIG(0) part of RFC 2535.

All of Section 4.1.8.1 of RFC 2535 is updated, along with parts of Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Nothing in the document changes the KEY or NXT resource records, or the processing involved in data origin and denial authentication for DNS data.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier specification of this signature was wrong in small ways that break interoperability with existing software, so those parts are replaced here.

sections.title: Why SIG(0) Exists
sections.content:
SIG(0) provides protection for DNS transactions and requests that the regular SIG, KEY and NXT records of RFC 2535 do not. The authenticated data origin services of secure DNS either protect data resource records or authentically deny their nonexistence. They give no protection for glue records, none for DNS requests, none for the message headers of requests or responses, and none for the overall integrity of a response.

Transaction authentication means that a requester can be sure it is at least getting the messages from the server it queried, and that the messages it received are in response to the query it sent. It is done by adding, optionally, either a TSIG record or a SIG(0) record at the end of the response, which digitally signs the concatenation of the server's response and the corresponding resolver query. Requests can be authenticated the same way, by putting a special SIG(0) at the end of the request. Authenticating requests serves no purpose in DNS servers that predate dynamic update, and requests with a non-empty additional information section produce error returns or are even ignored by some of those older servers. The signing syntax exists for authenticating dynamic update requests, TKEY requests, and future requests that need authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIG(0) covers the whole exchange: the question and the answer together. That is what lets a client check that the reply really is the answer to its question and that nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: Keys and the Difference From TSIG
sections.content:
The private keys used in transaction security belong to the host that composes the DNS response message, not to the zone involved. Request authentication may also involve the private key of the host or other entity composing the request, or of a zone the request would affect. The matching public keys are normally stored in the DNS and retrieved as KEY records with a protocol byte of 3, for DNSSEC, or 255, for ANY.

Because requests and replies vary so much, message authentication signatures cannot be calculated in advance, so the private key has to be kept on line, in software or in directly connected hardware.

SIG(0) and TSIG differ in significant ways. TSIG uses secret keys installed at both ends, so the presence of such a key implies that the other party understands TSIG and very likely has the same key installed, and it uses keyed hash authentication codes that are relatively inexpensive to compute. It is therefore common to authenticate requests with TSIG, and to authenticate the response with TSIG if the request was authenticated that way.

SIG(0) uses public key authentication, with the public keys stored in the DNS as KEY records and the private key at the signer. A KEY record existing does not necessarily mean that SIG(0) is implemented. Verifying a SIG(0) means obtaining and checking the matching KEY, which can be expensive and slow. Signing every request and verifying it before responding can lead to a deadly embrace, where the KEY needed to verify one request has to be fetched with another signed request, and so on. Omitting the signature on requests that do not need it also halves the number of public key operations in the transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: TSIG shares a secret with the server and is cheap. SIG(0) uses a public key stored in the DNS, which is slower to check because the key may have to be fetched first.

sections.title: The SIG(0) Resource Record
sections.content:
The structure and type number of SIG records are given in RFC 2535, but all of Section 4.1.8.1 and the parts of Sections 4.2 and 4.3 that concern SIG(0) are replaced by this document. Any conflict between RFC 2535 and this document about SIG(0) records is resolved in favour of this document.

For every transaction SIG(0), the signer field must be the name of the originating host, and there must be a KEY record at that name holding the public key that matches the private key used to calculate the signature. The host name used may be the inverse IP address mapping name for an address of the host, if the relevant KEY is stored there.

For every SIG(0), the owner name, class, TTL and original TTL are meaningless. The TTL fields should be zero and the class field should be ANY, and to save space the owner name should be root, a single zero octet. When a signed response is wanted, the SIG(0) has the highest priority of any additional information for inclusion in the response. If it cannot be added without truncating the message, the server must alter the response so that a SIG(0) can be included: the response then holds only the question and a SIG(0) record, with the TC bit set and RCODE 0, which is NOERROR, and the client should then retry the request over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The record sits at the end of the message and most of its fields carry no meaning, so they are set to fixed values. If the signature does not fit in the message, the server sends back a short answer that tells the client to try again over TCP.

sections.title: Calculating Request and Transaction Signatures
sections.content:
A DNS request may be signed by putting one SIG(0) at the end of the additional information section of the query. Such a signature is identified by a type covered field of zero. It signs the preceding DNS request message, including the DNS header but not the UDP or IP header, and before the request record counts have been adjusted for the inclusion of the signature. The data signed is the RDATA of the SIG(0) with the signature subfield omitted entirely, not merely zeroed, followed by the request message: data = RDATA | request - SIG(0).

A SIG(0) can also secure a response together with the request that produced it. The data signed is then the RDATA without the signature, the entire query message including its DNS header but not its UDP or IP header, and the entire response message including its header but not its UDP or IP header, and before the response record counts have been adjusted for the inclusion of the signature: data = RDATA | full query | response - SIG(0).

Checking a response signature, which is signed by the server host key and not by the zone key, shows that the query and the response were not tampered with in transit, that the response corresponds to the intended query, and that the response came from the queried server.

For a DNS message over TCP, the SIG(0) on the first data packet is calculated as above, and for each later packet the data is data = RDATA | DNS payload - SIG(0) | previous packet, where the previous packet is the previous DNS payload including its header and its SIG(0) but not the TCP or IP header. Support of SIG(0) over TCP is optional; TSIG may be used instead, setting up a key with TKEY if needed. A request and a response can have either a single TSIG or one SIG(0), but never both.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature covers the record's own data plus the messages themselves. For a reply it covers the question as well, and for a long reply over TCP each packet covers the one before it.

sections.title: Checking Signatures and Lifetime
sections.content:
If a SIG record sits at the end of the additional information section of a response and has a type covered of zero, it is a transaction signature covering the response and the query that produced it. For TKEY responses it must be checked and the message rejected if the checks fail, unless the TKEY mode in use says otherwise. For all other responses it may be checked, and the message rejected if the checks fail.

A successful transaction signature does not directly authenticate the validity of any data records in the message. What it does authenticate is that those records were sent by the queried server and were not tampered with. Only a proper SIG(0) signed by the zone, or by a key tracing its authority to the zone or to static resolver configuration, can directly authenticate the data records, depending on resolver policy. A resolver or server that does not implement transaction or request signatures must ignore them without error where they are optional, and treat them as failures where they are required.

The inception and expiration times in a SIG(0) exist to resist replay attacks. They should form a time bracket so that messages outside it are ignored, and in IP networks that bracket should not normally extend further than 5 minutes into the past or 5 minutes into the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking the signature proves the reply came from the server and was not changed, but it does not prove that the records inside it are correct. The times on the signature make an old copy of the message useless.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are no additional considerations beyond those in RFC 2535. The one change the RFC notes is that the inception and expiration time of the SIG(0) are now covered by the signature, which improves resistance to replay attacks. The document creates no new parameters and assigns no new parameter values.

The appendix lists the changes from RFC 2535: the explanatory text about the differences between TSIG and SIG(0), the requirement that the TTL fields be zero, the class field be ANY and the owner name be root, the rules on calculating the signature, and the rules on the lifetime of a SIG(0).
sections.plainLanguage: The security rules are the ones from the earlier specification. The one addition is that the valid time window is now signed, so an old message cannot be replayed.

viz.caption: What the plain secure DNS records leave unprotected

items.title: DNS requests
items.text: Nothing protects a request from being forged or altered.

items.title: Message headers
items.text: Neither the headers of requests nor of responses are protected.

items.title: Glue records
items.text: The records that glue a delegation into the zone are not covered.

items.title: Overall response integrity
items.text: Nothing shows that the whole reply is unaltered and belongs to the query.
